summary: This chunk adds two new files: a red-team report on a session pricing-cache design, and the author's notes/assumptions. The report lists 13 numbered findings (F-01 to F-13) against a Redis-based pricing cache, rated Critical/High/Medium/Low, each with a fix direction. Three Criticals center on wrong-price risk: a dangerous `KEYS` mass-delete, missing invalidation for catalog/tax changes, and no stated re-pricing at charge time. Highs cover thundering-herd invalidation, mid-session staleness, memory headroom, a kill switch that depends on the same Redis, and downsized downstream capacity post-rollout. A re-check protocol with per-ID pass criteria closes the report. The notes file states assumptions: no live user, arch-review audience, and that numbers in fix directions are conventional, not measured.

claims.text: `KEYS session:*:pricing` is O(N), blocks the Redis event loop, and can stall rate-limiting and feature-flag reads on the shared cluster
On Redis Cluster, `KEYS` only sees one node per call, so mass-delete is incomplete as well as dangerous
The design's invalidation section covers promos only, leaving catalog price and tax-rate changes stale for up to 30 minutes with no fix
The doc never states that the charge/confirm path re-prices from source of truth, so cache staleness could translate into wrong charges, not just wrong quotes
Full invalidation of ~200k session entries causes a simultaneous fan-out miss storm to catalog, promo, and tax services sized only for cache-miss traffic
Promos that expire mid-session (e.g. flash sale ending) keep applying from cache until TTL, because `promo_changed` may not fire for time-based expiry
The cache key is session-ID only, so mid-session changes to shipping address (tax) or coupon/cart contents (promo) are not reflected until the entry expires
40KB per session times 200k sessions equals 8GB, exactly the stated free capacity, leaving no headroom for per-key overhead, replication, or fragmentation
The rollback kill switch is a feature flag served from the same Redis cluster the design is meant to protect, so it may be unusable during the incident it's meant to stop

Post-rollout, downstream services are sized for cache-miss traffic only, so a Redis outage delivers a full-traffic step function to now-undersized services, and without a circuit breaker each request first burns a Redis timeout, raising p95 rather than restoring it
The doc names no delivery guarantee, consumer-lag alert, or reconciliation for the `promo_changed` event, so a missed event leaves stale promos undetected
A one-day 5%-then-100% rollout cannot surface memory footprint, invalidation herd size, or a promo publish/Redis blip, and defines no success/abort criteria or metrics
The cached hash has no schema version, so a deploy changing its layout risks silent misparse of pricing data

First-quote caching stores whatever the downstream calls return, including degraded/partial results, freezing them for 30 minutes; concurrent first quotes both write, which is harmless but worth noting
Numbers used in fix directions (timeouts, headroom fractions) are conventional starting points, not measured values, and pass criteria require the doc's own measured numbers
The review was performed directly without invoking the `debate-review` skill because the output directory is a `without_skill` baseline

risks.note: The 40KB-per-session and 200k-session figures used to compute the 8GB memory estimate are not shown in this chunk; they appear to come from the target design doc, which this chunk doesn't include.
The 480ms baseline p95 figure is referenced as a comparison point but its source isn't shown in this chunk.
The claim that downstream services will be 'sized for ~cache-miss traffic only' post-rollout is asserted as a prediction about future capacity planning, not evidenced in this chunk.

least_confident: Whether the 40KB/200k-session/8GB memory figures in F-07 accurately reflect the underlying design doc, since that doc isn't part of this chunk and I can't verify the arithmetic's inputs.
